name: The earlier mnevo
summary: From 2018 to 2022 this organization held earlier attempts under the name mnevo: a Vue and Node web application (mnevo, mnevo-server, mnevo-licuha) and its documentation with an architecture diagram (mnevo-docs).
why: History to learn from before designing again.

name: The memory kingdom
summary: The engine reflects the kingdom of memory a person builds in their mind with those techniques - its places, images and links - so it can be seen, walked and tended.
why: What is built only in the head fades unseen; reflected, it can be kept.

name: Mnemonic Vocabulary
summary: A graphical, interactive vocabulary engine for all mnemonic and visual-mnemonic techniques.
why: The techniques work, but each person rebuilds them alone and in their head; an engine can hold them, teach them and keep what was built.

name: One core, many devices
summary: It runs on Linux - a PC and a smartphone - and maybe on Android; the core is the same everywhere.
why: A person's memory work should go with them.

name: Refreshing at the best intervals
summary: The engine helps to refresh memories: it brings each one back for re-practice at the best interval.
why: A memory repeated at the right moment lasts; at the wrong one it is lost or wasted.

name: The techniques
summary: How to encode numbers, foreign words and any information into images and places - every mnemonic technique as something the engine knows, shows and lets a person practise.
why: A vocabulary of techniques, not one method.

name: Scenes as evidence
summary: A scene is an interaction written down - keys pressed, screens expected - run on every change; its screens are kept as evidence a person can look at.
why: An interactive tool should be proven like any other: by a machine, every time.

name: Two doors
summary: Every tool keeps an interactive door for people and a structured door - plain arguments, readable output - for agents and scripts. The driver is for checking the interactive door, not for everyday use.
why: An agent pressing keys on a screen is slow and brittle; a structured door is neither. argenv's own idea - one setting, two doors - applied to whole tools.

name: Automate what you do twice by hand
statement: The second time a manual step is repeated, build the tool, document it in the repository's agent notes and log, and use cheap compute (CI) where it can. The ship script, the gate, the splitter, the scans and the timing report each began as a step done by hand twice.

name: Release in batches, not on every merge
statement: A release per merge costs minutes of waiting and gives users a new version every few minutes, while proving little that CI does not. Release when about ten changes wait, or the oldest has waited a week, or a change touches how releases are *published* (the one thing only a release proves), or on request. Make the policy a small tested function.

name: One branch, one merged pull request per iteration
statement: Each iteration is a branch from the current main, a pull request whose body says what and why and shows the evidence, and a squash merge with a conventional title. History reads as the story of the work, and nothing depends on a conversation.

name: Check the property, not the symptom
statement: A compile, a green build or a passing test is not the check that a change did what you meant. Check the property itself: that no string literal changed under a rename, that the output is byte-identical, that the real program says what you think it says. Almost every surprise in this project was a symptom taken for the property.

name: The levers that paid
statement: A prebuilt tool instead of compiling it; a timeout on every job; the cache saved only from main; narrower triggers so a documents-only change skips the heavy jobs; no incremental builds or full debug info in CI; retries on the network. A policy swap (here, the audit's rules) was proven locally against a known-bad case before it replaced the old one.

name: Decide, following the canon and the project's interest
statement: An agent given a principle decides, and says what it decided and why, instead of handing the choice back. It asks only when the answer needs something it cannot know, and it checks between iterations that each action still serves the purpose and is not busy work.

name: Documents are checked against the code
statement: A document that names a path is checked to name a real one; a code example in a document is compared with the source; a page about how close the code is to the ideal says where it is not close. A guess written as fact is corrected in writing when it turns out wrong, and so is an invented date.

name: A fast local gate; CI for the rest
statement: One command runs what must pass before shipping (format, lint, docs, links, licences, tests), writes each step's log to a file and prints one line per step. CI runs the heavy matrix. The gate is for reproducing a failure and for catching mistakes early, not a substitute for the pull request.

name: Findability as a test
statement: Generate an outline from every module's first sentence, then ask it real questions in a test ("where is it said which kind of disk we work with?") and fail if the answer is not near the top. A cold read, turned into something that runs on every change. If a description is vague, or a thing is in the wrong place, it shows here first.

name: Generalise a tool with a parity test
statement: When a script built for one project is made general, run the general one and the original on the original's own project and compare the results. If they differ, form a hypothesis and test it with a controlled experiment (give the new one the old one's exact rule and see whether the results then match) until every difference is explained and deliberate. A generalisation that is 'about the same' has changed something nobody chose.

name: Pin the real output
statement: Record the exact text of the program's commands on a real fixture, and fail CI when it differs. A change to wording then shows as the few lines that moved, reviewed as such. Re-record only after reading the diff: a recording of empty output looks as clean as a good one until you read it.

name: Guards are tests that read the source
statement: Architecture rules are ordinary tests that read the source tree (or its parsed form) and fail naming the file and line. A rule that lives only in a document is a wish; a rule that fails the build is a property of the project.

name: Look around first
statement: Before acting, take a clear look at the situation: what is, what we are dealing with, why it is so, and what others already learned. Keep what was found as research - the question, the findings, their sources - so the decisions that rest on it can cite it, and anyone can follow a step down to what it stands on.

name: Look at what people will see
statement: A check that a page answers, or that every link on it resolves, cannot see that it looks wrong. Look at it the way a reader will: a screenshot of the real page in a real browser, of the live site and not only of a local build. Three defects of this playbook's own site (literals not styled as code, a table of contents drawn like the navigation bar, headings drawn as links) were visible only that way.

name: Measure before you claim
statement: Say how long, how many, how big, before and after, with the samples, and say when the samples overlap. A claim chosen from the best runs is not a measurement. When you find you overclaimed, retract it in writing, where the claim was made.

name: Measure the CI before optimising it
statement: Collect wall time, job-minutes and the slowest jobs and steps over several runs, then change the critical path. The biggest win here was one step, a security audit that compiled its own tool for three minutes. Reject, with reasons, what the measurement does not support.

name: Names explain the program
statement: Names of files, folders, actions and states say what the thing is for, in plain words. Folders are named for what the program is *for*, not for how it is built (`going_back/`, not `adapters/`). A part's first sentence says what it is for without a pattern word like adapter or port.

name: Judge CI by the newest run of each check
statement: Reruns and flakes leave old failures in the history. Judge a commit by the newest run of each check name, count skipped as passing, and rerun a job the runner itself failed to start. A release is the commit titled as one, not the merge before it.

name: A fact, a word or a rule lives in one place
statement: A sentence a person reads, a plural, a rule about disks, a way of counting: written once, in the layer that owns it, and used everywhere. Every copy is a place it can come out differently. Guards forbid the copy, and a helper makes the one place cheap to use.

name: Report in plain words, at the big picture
statement: Say what changed, how much closer it is to the ideal, what went wrong, and what is next, in language a person who does not read the code can follow. Technical detail belongs in the log and the pull request. Own mistakes briefly and say what they taught.

name: Prove every guard bites
statement: A guard that has only ever passed is unproven. Break the thing it guards on purpose, in a clean file, confirm it fails with a useful message, then restore the file *exactly* (and compare). Two checks can pass together for the wrong reason, for example a link and its target both wrong in the same way, so test the rule against the outside truth too.

name: Published identities are not renamed for a word
statement: A key in a JSON output, a contract's identity, a stored word in a journal: other programs and older files read them. Give people a plain word beside the stored one, test both, and leave the stored one alone, with the reason written down.

name: Remove a race by construction
statement: A rare failure is not disproved by many clean runs on a fast machine. Find the shared resource, put every use behind one lock, and show with a stress test that the original fails and the fixed version does not.

name: Debts are data and only shrink
statement: A rule that cannot be met today is recorded as a number per file in a data file. The test fails if any number grows, and insists the file record any decrease. Progress cannot silently slip back, and what remains is a list anyone can read.

name: A stateless, resumable shipper
statement: One script pushes, opens the pull request, waits for checks, merges and verifies. It keeps no state of its own, reading GitHub every time, and it stops itself before the tool's time limit with a code that means *run me again*. Any session can continue what another began.

name: Retire a word with a guard
statement: When a word is wrong (here, *config* for an area), rename its uses with a lexer-based tool that follows string interpolation and verifies no literal changed, then add a guard that the word is not an identifier outside the adapter that owns it.

name: Say what to do next, once
statement: Every situation where nothing is there, or something failed, says what to do about it, in the layer that owns the words, so every surface (command line, window) is equally helpful and none repeats it differently.

name: Search by shape, and read all of the results
statement: To find a smell, search by its *shape* (every bare bool in a pair, every `if n == 1`), not by the instance you noticed. Read the whole result: a search cut off after ten lines once hid the one script that pinned a change, and CI found it.

name: Seeded cold reads
statement: Pick modules at random with a seed (so the read is reproducible), read them as a stranger, and write down where you stumbled. It finds what no guard measures: a rule copied by hand, a stale word, a distinction the code makes and never names. It stops paying when a seed returns modules you have already read; that is the signal to read differently.

name: Each layer is a small language
statement: A layer offers a vocabulary (types, verbs, nouns) and the layer above is written in it. A command reads as a story of those words: look, ask, begin, do, end, show. The reader meets the story first and the mechanism only when they ask.

name: State and plans live in the repository
statement: An agent's memory is not the project's memory. The plan (backlog), the decisions (log), the rules (agent notes) and the documentation of the tools are files in the repository, so no session starts over and any agent can continue where another stopped.

name: The stranger test
statement: Someone who has never seen the code should be able to say what a part is for from its first line, and be right. It is the measure of clarity, and the only one that cannot be gamed by moving code around.

name: Tools that rewrite code verify themselves
statement: A splitter, a renamer or a formatter that edits many files checks its own work: every comment survives, no string literal changed, nothing is written unless everything matches. A regex rename once changed a JSON key and a fake tool's output; a lexer-based one that verifies the strings changed none.

name: Every layer is the top of the layers beneath it
statement: Read from the top, each part says what it is *for*, in the words a person uses; each step down says *how*, using only the words of the layer beneath it. You can stop at any level and still understand the program, and you never have to hold all of it in your head. This is the one idea the rest of the playbook serves.

name: Two faces: what it is for, and a body in the words beneath
statement: Every part has an upward face (its purpose, and the words it offers) and a downward face (a body written only in the words of the layers below). A part that cannot be described that way is doing two jobs, and is split.

name: Use the program as a newcomer would
statement: Run the real program on a real disk, from first use to going back, and read every word it says; drive a terminal UI through a pseudo-terminal and print its screens. Reading code finds what is wrong with code; only using the program finds what is wrong with what it *says*.

name: Words are decisions
statement: Choose each word as a decision: look at what others call the thing and what the reader already knows, prefer the plain word with one meaning, and keep the choice with the words rejected and the reasons. One language, used the same way in talk, in code and in documents.

name: Additive-only file structure
statement: Rhizoid-managed metadata (manifest, sync state) is added as new files alongside upstream's own, never edited in place inside upstream's existing files. This keeps a pull from upstream conflict-free for the tracked branch - not a guarantee that any patch to upstream code stays conflict-free, only that Rhizoid's own bookkeeping never collides with it.

name: Adopt an existing fork vs create a new one
statement: Two different, deliberately separate operations: rhizoid add forks a new copy of upstream; rhizoid import points at a fork that already exists (with or without the rhizoid wrapper already on it) and adopts it into the manifest without creating anything. Kept as two verbs rather than one flag with a default, the way terraform keeps import separate from apply - the two operations have different blast radii and a wrong default in either direction is a real mistake (an unwanted duplicate fork, or silently overwriting someone's existing, satisfactory fork).

name: argenv declares flags and env vars - not subcommands or positionals
statement: Read argenv's own source and README before designing against it: it is explicitly "a declared, typed contract for a program's invocation surface - argv and envp", and every Input it declares binds to a --flag/env-var pair, never a bare positional value. Confirmed by reading argenv-cli's own main.rs (the author's own reference CLI): subcommand dispatch is a plain match on args.first(), not anything argenv provides. Rhizoid's CLI follows the same shape: a thin hand-written dispatcher picks the verb and reads each command's one primary positional (a repo spec, a URL, a module name) directly; argenv declares only the named flags for each verb.

name: Auth: shell out to gh, for now
statement: Rhizoid calls the GitHub CLI (gh) for anything needing authentication - forking, merge-upstream, reading repo state - rather than managing its own token or OAuth flow. Whoever already has gh authenticated can use Rhizoid immediately; the tool has no credentials of its own to store, rotate, or leak. Revisit if a use case needs something gh cannot do (a non-GitHub git host, for one).

name: Clean patch back upstream
statement: Because Rhizoid's own metadata never touches upstream's files, a diff of the patch branch against the pristine tracking branch is a clean patch, submittable as a normal PR to the original repo, whether or not its owner has ever heard of Rhizoid.

name: No central lockfile - state is distributed into each fork
statement: Cargo, npm, Poetry and Nix all pair a human-edited manifest with a separate, machine-written lockfile recording exact resolved state. Rhizoid does not need a top-level lockfile: each managed fork is already a real git repository with its own history, and its own .rhizoid/module.toml already carries that module's exact recorded state (see [module-metadata-file](concepts.md#module-metadata-file)). A central lockfile would just be a second, independently-driftable copy of information git already holds per-repo.

name: Status detects drift, not just reports the manifest
statement: rhizoid status inspects the real state of every managed fork (does it exist, what commit is the tracking branch actually at, is there uncommitted or unmanifested structure) and diffs that against the manifest's record, the way terraform plan diffs real infrastructure against Terraform state. The manifest is a record of intent, not a source of truth Rhizoid trusts blindly - reality always wins the comparison.

name: Fork destination is a manifest setting, not hardcoded
statement: Where a new fork lands (which org or account) is configured per manifest, with a default and a per-module override - the same shape as west's remotes list (a named set of url-bases) plus each project's optional remote: override. Nothing about Rhizoid assumes forks live in one specific org.

name: The manifest is TOML, with the footgun that argues against it named up front
statement: TOML: native comments (unlike JSON), no implicit type coercion or indentation sensitivity (unlike YAML - see [the YAML document from hell](sources.md#yaml-document-from-hell)), and its array-of-tables syntax is a direct fit for "a list of modules, each a flat record". Cross-ecosystem adoption for exactly this kind of file (a hand-editable project/tool manifest, not a deeply-nested orchestration config) is real and independent of any one language: Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, Hugo, Netlify. The honest counter-case: Cloudflare's Wrangler shipped TOML-only for years, then added JSONC and now recommends it for new projects, naming TOML's array-of-tables syntax as a real footgun in practice - a misplaced or missing [[table]] header silently puts a value in the wrong entry (see [the future of Wrangler configuration](sources.md#wrangler-toml-to-jsonc)). That risk is highest when a file is mostly hand-typed from scratch, which is not the common case here: the manifest is meant to be edited through add/import/remove, not freehand, and each module's own detailed state lives in its own .rhizoid/module.toml rather than piling many [[module]] entries into one large hand-edited file - closer to Cargo.toml's [dependencies] table (mostly tool-written) than to a large hand-maintained Wrangler config.

name: Each fork carries its own .rhizoid/module.toml
statement: The additive metadata that makes a fork "attached" lives in a new .rhizoid/module.toml file at the fork's own root: origin URL, tracked ref, pinned commit, whether it was added or imported, when. Mirrors .tad/.gitrepo's pattern from the tad system - a plain, readable file is the source of truth for state, not something buried in commit messages or a separate database.

name: The v1 command surface: init, add, import, update, status, refresh, remove
statement: init sets up a manifest. add forks a new module into the configured org and starts tracking it. import adopts an existing fork without creating one. update pulls upstream into a module's tracking branch (GitHub's merge-upstream). status reports drift between the manifest and real git/GitHub state. refresh reconciles the manifest to match observed reality without changing anything (mirrors terraform apply -refresh-only) - this is how a by-hand change gets folded back in rather than flagged as drift forever. remove drops a module from the manifest. send-upstream (clean patch back to the true upstream) is real but deferred to v0.2, after the core loop is proven.

name: Two crates: rhizoid-core and rhizoid-cli
statement: Mirrors argenv's own workspace shape (crates/argenv + crates/argenv-cli). rhizoid-core holds the Manifest and Module types, their JSON Schema (via schemars, the same crate argenv itself already uses for its own contract feature), and the GitPort/GitHubPort traits the real fork/sync logic will implement later. rhizoid-cli holds argv dispatch and the per-command argenv Models. Splitting now, before there is much code, avoids a disruptive later refactor once the planned TUI needs to depend on the same core logic without the CLI.

name: Rhizoid-cutting (rhizcut)
statement: A single dependency managed by Rhizoid: a real GitHub fork of an upstream repo, owned and pinned rather than referenced remotely. Named after a horticultural cutting - a piece taken from a parent plant and rooted separately, genetically identical at the start but independent from then on.

name: Tracking branch vs patch branch
statement: The branch that mirrors upstream is never hand-edited - only fast-forwarded via merge-upstream. All customization lives on a separate branch that merges from the tracking branch. The tracking branch never conflicts; the patch branch might, exactly once, when upstream touches a line you also patched - that is inherent to patching, not a tooling failure.

name: One baseline per device
summary: Every check that ever passed is held to; a check outside a run's scope is not asked, rather than kept in a second baseline.
why: Two baselines would be two truths about one phone.

name: The conveyor refuses what cannot work
summary: Each mistake that cost a try becomes a refusal with a reason: a kernel that is not an EFI program, a listening test without the word that the microphone is placed.
why: A refusal costs a second; a lost try costs a reboot and a wrong theory.

name: Read the device's own record first
summary: Before cleaning up after an experiment, read what the device itself recorded: a boot entry's try counter, the bootloader's selection, the crash memory.
why: Three theories about the bootloader were wrong; the entry's counter settled it in one look.

name: A placed microphone gives relative levels
summary: A microphone placed by the phone tells which speaker is louder from where it stands, and whether there is sound at all - not absolute loudness.
why: Honest about what the instrument can say.

name: The phone is the reference
summary: Kept in a known-working state at all times: every experiment is one try that falls back by itself, and the phone is checked well before and after.
why: A reference that drifts cannot tell a regression from a mistake.

name: Chainability
summary: One project's data can feed another's - device tests into a grand project's path, a tool's releases into a lab's - each row carrying where it came from.
why: An ecosystem, not a heap: data flows along the real relations between projects.

name: Data made by work
summary: A project's data is produced by its work - commits, builds, tests, releases - not typed up afterwards; what only a person can supply is written once, where the work happens.
why: Records kept by hand are kept late, wrong, or not at all.

name: Manual-work saturation
summary: A project's ledger of small actions done by hand, each counted. Doing one again bumps its count; past three it is saturated and asks for a tool. A record automated by a tool says so - and a later bump asks why it was done by hand again. Deliberate hand-work (looking, listening, deciding) is counted but never asks. Saturation is effort, not only count: minutes weighted by load (0-10, Borg CR10).
why: Practice 20 says build the tool when the same hand-work comes a third time; nothing counted the times. The ledger is the counter, and the observatory sums it across projects to show where one shared tool would serve many.

name: Data made by work
summary: A project's data is produced by its development and its functioning - commits, builds, tests, releases, measurements - as a principle and by tools, never kept by hand.
why: Hand-kept data goes stale and lies; data made by work is as true as the work.

name: The observatory is a mirror
summary: Projects produce their data; the observatory reads it. Everything breathes through ocoeco - its language, gatherers and checks - and no project needs the observatory to work.
why: A mirror that projects depend on becomes a single point of failure.

name: One language, so the pieces join
summary: Plain text tables, a mark, shared names for the common things (idea, path, workings, work), and data that feeds other projects' data with its origin on every line.
why: Without one language nothing can be gathered or compared.

name: Prior art travels with the ideas
summary: A project's sources are what people already learned that it stands on, and what it takes from each; concepts and decisions cite them, so the research behind an idea is seen where the idea is.
why: Asked by the author: take the best humanity has to offer into account, and let it propagate through everything.

name: Look around first
summary: Before acting: what is, what we are dealing with, why it is so, and what others already learned - kept as research (the question, what was found, its sources), cited by the decisions that rest on it, shown beside the steps those decisions are about.
why: No action is complete if it does not begin with a clear look at the situation. The chain research, decision, step lets anyone follow a step down to what it rests on.

name: Research has versions
summary: A refresh adds a new version and never overwrites; earlier versions stay one click away. Views of facts follow the latest version; a decision keeps citing the version it rested on, and says when a newer one exists.
why: A decision made on old research should say so, not silently appear to rest on new findings.

name: tad, the format
summary: Text as data - tables as JSON lines with a schema, a canonical form and verification - is the format ocoeco speaks.
why: Readable by people, diffable by git, checkable by machines.

name: Three ways of knowing
summary: Live: gathered from a marked project as its work happens - the default, unmarked. Researched: taken from outside the commons, dated, with how it was found and its sources - shown outlined, with its age, linking to the research. Unknown: neither, and said so.
why: The author: let what others achieved fill the picture so it does not look empty to a newcomer - while making plain how we know each thing, and how fresh it is.

name: A vocabulary every project speaks
summary: Each project keeps its words and their exact meaning - what a word means in plain language, what it is not, what it is easily confused with. ocoeco defines the shared words (mark, lens, essence, working, cutting, conveyor...); projects inherit them and add their own; a redefined shared word is flagged. Shown as a page, and as the terms underlined in the project's own pages with their meaning beside them.
why: Concepts say what a project rests on; a vocabulary says what its words mean. Without it the words drift into dialects and live only in the heads that coined them.

name: Attention: where the whole is weakest
summary: One view across every project, computed from their data: steps nothing delivers, work in progress that has not moved, regressions, and what waits on a person (a merge, a SIM card). Read at the end of every stretch to choose the next.
why: Looking at the full picture should be a mechanism, not a mood.

name: The board
summary: A project's live work - ongoing, waiting, planned - kept as data and shown in the picture next to its path.
why: What is being done now, next to where it leads.

name: The conveyor
summary: A forkable lab that holds everything a person or an agent needs to bring a goal about - for phones: tools, procedures, safety rules, principles; projects made from it carry the mark.
why: Anyone can join with no setup and contribute back; every project fits the picture by construction.

name: Discovery, hexagonal
summary: Finding projects is a port; each platform is an outlet - GitHub first, others (GitLab, Open Hub) later without touching the core.
why: The observatory is not tied to one platform.

name: Essence
summary: Both a method and the observatory's signature view. The method (its own project, creation-guidelines/essence-oco): how to say why and how of anything, as four answers each leading to the next - why it exists, what it must reach, how each step is delivered and proven, what is happening now - with the test of a good answer for each; it describes itself with nothing but itself. The view: a project's landing page, the chain down one line, with four marks for how completely it tells its essence.
why: The format (ocoeco) and the drawing (the engine) do not say why to describe a process this way or how to do it well; and a chain read in four tabs is not seen.

name: A grand project's family
summary: The grand project's repository and every project whose parent is its owner or itself.
why: Each grand project's views show its own projects' data, and only theirs.

name: Grand project
summary: A marked project of kind picture: a large aim with its own tab, views and family of projects (Linux Phones is the first).
why: The observatory's navigation follows the commons' great aims, not any one of their parts.

name: The harvest
summary: On a schedule, the observatory reads every marked project's shared tables, tags each row with its project and merges them; problems are shown, not lost.
why: The picture keeps itself current.

name: How we work, as a working set
summary: Not a manifest but a usable set under one roof (the creation-guidelines organization): how to think - the canon's principles and architectures, the ideal project - and how to do - the practices, each naming the tool that carries it (land, shot, ocoeco check, lab-agent-oco) - shown as a lens like any other, and reachable by anyone through one command.
why: A practice that rests on memory is weaker than one a tool enforces; and a way of working others cannot pick up is only ours.

name: Languages
summary: Two kinds of text, each translated where it belongs: the interface in the face's Fluent catalogs (grammar and plural forms right), the data in each project's translations table (marked human or machine), falling back to the source. The site is the same static files per language under /<language>/, switched by a thin line of languages by their own names.
why: A commons is read in many languages; translating where the text belongs keeps sources clean and translations honest.

name: Lens
summary: A repository of its own (kind lens) that declares a family of projects and the views that show it - from a small shared vocabulary (path, matrix, families, runs, backlog, log, ideas, heartbeat, cards). The observatory discovers lenses and renders each with the same engine; curated lenses take its navigation, every other is listed among the discovered.
why: Views hard-coded in the observatory made it a gatekeeper; lenses let anyone make a grand view of their own family of projects, built exactly as the observatory's own.

name: The mark
summary: oco.toml at a repository's root plus the oco-project topic (and oco-kind-<kind>): which project it is, its kind, its parent, the tables it shares.
why: A repository becomes a piece of the picture by itself; discovery is one search of GitHub's index.

name: Milestone
summary: A stop on a project's path, on one horizon, with criteria tied to measured data (feature statuses, tests, health); it fills by itself as evidence arrives, never by hand.
why: Progress that cannot be argued with: each step says what proves it.

name: The observatory
summary: A meta structure, tied to no project: one living picture of every project of the open commons, built from the projects' own data.
why: So the commons can be seen whole, and every project's place in it, without anyone keeping the picture by hand.

name: The observer
summary: Half-manual tests ask an observer - a person today, a rig of cameras and servos later - with nothing else changing.
why: Tests that need eyes and hands still run as a conveyor.

name: ocoeco
summary: The observatory's information ecosystem and its backbone - both a principle (data is produced by projects as they are made and as they work, never by hand) and a tool (formats and protocols, gatherers, chaining, propagation), in the repository ocoeco.
why: It is the working system of the whole picture; naming it makes it something to design and tend.

name: The path
summary: A project's visit card: a line through its three horizons, its milestones as stops, filled to where the evidence shows - and unknown shown as unknown.
why: One view that says where a project is and what is next, beautifully, for every project the same way.

name: The readiness ladder
summary: Under the horizons, a project's maturity on the established Technology Readiness Levels (concept to proven in operation), so projects of any kind compare on one scale.
why: An established, project-agnostic scale, rather than one invented here.

name: Shared parts as rhizcuts
summary: tad, the mark and the conveyor's tools travel as rhizoid modules: owned, patchable git forks rather than template copies or subtrees.
why: Transparent dependencies that click in like puzzle pieces and send fixes back.

name: tad, the heart
summary: tad - text as data - is the living heart and blood of oco-eco: the formats every project's data is kept in, the gatherers that fill them, the views that show them; supplied in every repository as a rhizcut.
why: Everything the observatory shows flows through tad.

name: Text as data (tad)
summary: Everything a project knows - plans, decisions, concepts, progress, measurements - is kept as tad data in its own repository, and rendered from there.
why: Nothing important lives only in a person's or an agent's memory; anyone can pick up where others left off.

name: Three horizons
summary: Every project is measured against three: working (it does its job end to end), perfection (complete and polished - as good as it should be), ongoing perfection (it stays so: healthy, free of regressions, upstreamed, maintained).
why: One percentage hides where a project stands; three honest horizons show how close it is to working, to perfect, and to staying perfect.

name: Unknown is not failure
summary: What has not been measured is shown as not known yet - never counted as missing or broken.
why: Honest pictures: a gap in knowledge is work to do, not a verdict.

name: Replace a guess with a calculation
summary: Which version is this, what does it need, does it need rebuilding, do these conflict, what may it touch, who is affected by this flaw, are these two things the same: each is guessed today and becomes a calculation once things have stable identities.
why: It is the whole idea; everything else is engineering.

name: The three mistakes, and the one beneath
summary: Things are identified by name; versions describe whole components; boundaries are treated as walls - and beneath all three, isolation is the default and connection is work. All inherited from tape drives that read one file at a time, never designed.
why: Software interacts: that is what it is for. Connection should be the default, isolation the declared exception.

name: Identity by what a thing is
summary: A definition is identified by a fingerprint computed from its own contents plus the fingerprints of everything it depends on (a Merkle tree; mutually dependent groups are fingerprinted together). Names become labels pointing at fingerprints.
why: Rename, move, reorganise - nothing breaks; and 'is this, and everything beneath it, exactly the same?' is answered by one number.

name: Structure, not text
summary: The fingerprint is computed from the structure of the code - formatting, spacing and the names of internal variables fall away (alpha-equivalence). Two people making the same change in different styles produce the same fingerprint.
why: Identical work is recognised as one thing and stored once. The honest limit: different methods reaching the same answer are never recognised as identical.

name: The graph is the source of truth
summary: What is stored, hashed, compared and edited is resolved structure. Text appears once on the way in and once on the way out, at one marked boundary; nowhere between is text anything but a derived rendering.
why: Lose this and it becomes git with hashes without anyone noticing the day it happened.

name: There are no files
summary: With every reference a fingerprint, imports have no job, and then files have none: there is a graph of definitions and links, looked at through views - slices you choose and switch between, typing ordinary code, navigating relationships instead of folders. Your layout is remembered as yours; authors may suggest a reading order.
why: A relationship can hide in files; in a view computed from real relationships it is in front of you by default.

name: The closure
summary: Start from what you want, follow every reference, stop when nothing new appears: exactly what is needed, nothing more.
why: You take the behaviour, not the box it shipped in.

name: Grafting
summary: Taking a piece of someone else's software into yours: its closure arrives, attaches, and remembers where it came from so improvements can go home. Wrap what exists, replace it gradually underneath.
why: One function arrives as eleven definitions you can read, not a library with three hundred and forty dependencies.

name: Changing is not editing
summary: A changed thing is a different thing with a different fingerprint; the original stands and its users are unaffected. The chain above re-points with small records - 'same as before, except this reference' - bounded by your project. A succession link notes lineage.
why: It deletes version numbers, dependencies as commonly understood, and merge conflicts: 'I fixed it in my fork' becomes a stable end state that costs nothing.

name: Frozen, with a path to fixes
summary: Nothing updates unless you say so - which also means nothing is silently fixed. So: who is affected is a lookup; a fix arrives classified (drop-in, needs conversion, needs a rebuild); and per item you pin, follow, or defer to someone you trust. When two you trust disagree, you are shown both.
why: Resolve disagreement automatically and everyone converges on whichever authority is fastest - a central gatekeeper rebuilt.

name: Layers that can only add
summary: Architectures, bindings, shims, features: each an additive piece with a condition on it, inert unless the condition holds - never fetched, never built, structurally unable to break anyone it does not apply to.
why: A maintainer can accept a contribution without checking whether it breaks everyone else.

name: No configuration files
summary: Arguments, environment variables, configuration files and build flags exist because the finished program is a sealed box. A value is another item in the graph; configuring is pointing a reference elsewhere. Authors mark intended settings as exposed; some values genuinely arrive only at runtime.
why: There is nothing left to smuggle in.

name: Secrets as handles
summary: Secrets are never in the graph (nothing can be deleted from it, and fingerprints of short values can be reversed). The graph holds a handle resolved outside it when the program runs.
why: Rotation is free, handles can be weakened, revocation is instant - capability security.

name: Folklore becomes evidence
summary: A measurement attaches to the exact value it concerns, with its conditions - this hardware, this workload, this result - and because the configuration is exact, anyone who doubts it can reproduce it.
why: Advice about settings has always been untestable; what is worth trusting is the evidence and its conditions, never the number alone.

name: Stop searching the internet for your own computer
summary: Every exposed value carries its names, its author's default, its explanation in place, its lineage, what it affects and what others measured; search narrows to what you are actually running, and alternative names anyone adds become search terms.
why: Documentation rots because it is a copy of the truth; here there is one thing.

name: The program is a receipt
summary: The graph is the valuable thing; the program is a consequence recomputed from it, a cache entry nothing refers to. Understanding code is done once for everyone; preparing it for a machine is the cheaper half; only what actually changed rebuilds; results are stored by fingerprint too, so values sit beside the code.
why: One mechanism gives compilation caching, configuration and live values.

name: Everything visible, almost nothing present
summary: The machine appears to hold the entire tree of all software; a thing arrives the instant it is needed - done at the filesystem so every existing tool works unchanged.
why: Three organisations built this independently for their own codebases: the shape is forced, not arbitrary.

name: One kitchen, many dishes
summary: A long-running process keeps the shared groundwork warm; each program starts as a copy-on-write copy of it, in its own memory space.
why: The boundaries removed are filing conventions; the physical one that contains a crash stays.

name: Absent, not forbidden
summary: The list of pieces that built a program is its entire visible world: what it does not need is not denied to it - it is not there.
why: A sandbox nobody wrote and nobody can get wrong: it falls out of a calculation done for another reason.

name: Changing things while they run
summary: Calls go through an index of where each thing lives; replacing a thing is updating its entry. Whether a change can go live is computed beforehand: inside of a function - swap; shape of stored data - convert first; a boundary - restart.
why: Live updating stops being try-it-and-hope.

name: Rigor as a dial
summary: The same definitions expressed loosely - copying freely, vague errors, like a scripting language - or tightly - explicit ownership, no copying, precise types - tightened where a real wall is met; and tightening done once lives on the definition for everyone.
why: Working software on the first evening; learning driven by meeting a real limit.

name: Conjuring a shoot
summary: You do not install software: you point at the rhizome, draw a boundary, and a working shoot materialises. The shoot and its names are yours and die with the conjuring; only the changed substance goes home.
why: There is no dev environment and no separate kind of person: a user who hits a bug is already looking at what caused it.

name: It behaves like a living system
summary: Fingerprints are the genes and names the appearance; the Weismann barrier - the shape you drew and the name you gave stay yours, only substance is inherited; grafting is lateral gene transfer; renaming is a silent mutation; settings are gene regulation; disuse is how things die.
why: A model that keeps making correct predictions in a field it was not built for is probably carved along the real joints.

name: Assembly, not invention
summary: Every layer runs in production somewhere: structural identity (Unison), whole-tree-visible stores (Google, Microsoft, Meta), reversible slicing (josh), optional parts that stay unbuilt (the Linux kernel), fine-grained change analysis and edition morphing (Rust), the zygote model (Android), live patching (Linux).
why: Nobody has put them in the same room; and the patient authoring it needs has become cheap.

name: The first user ahead on day one
summary: The risk is not the engineering but adoption: the first person to use it must come out ahead at once, alone, with no community behind them.
why: Systems that asked people to invest first for a payoff later did not succeed.

name: Hypha
summary: The first milestone: the content-addressed core. It reads real Rust, fingerprints every definition by structure and dependencies, keeps them in one shared graph per machine, and turns a chosen piece back into running code (graft).
why: Three small steps - identity, graft, sync by difference - make a tool worth using on its own, and are the thesis made testable.
